blocks.text: A 67-year-old retired bus driver sits at 45 degrees on the couch. You turn his head gently to the left and see a pulsation behind his right sternocleidomastoid that rises well above his collarbone. Without any equipment, you have just estimated the pressure in his right atrium, and that is where the cardiovascular examination begins.

blocks.markdown: The cardiovascular examination is a structured routine: **general inspection and hands, pulse, blood pressure, jugular venous pressure (JVP), the precordium (inspection, palpation, auscultation) and finally the signs of heart failure** such as oedema. Following the same order every time means you do not forget parts of it. Each step is tied to anatomy: the JVP reflects right atrial pressure, the apex beat shows where the left ventricle strikes the chest wall, and the heart sounds mark valve closure.

blocks.title: Jugular venous pressure
blocks.text: The **JVP** is the vertical height of the column of blood in the internal jugular vein, measured above the sternal angle with the patient reclined at 45 degrees. It reflects right atrial pressure.

blocks.markdown:
### Pulses

Feel the **radial pulse** for rate and rhythm (count for at least 15 to 30 seconds), then the **brachial or carotid pulse** for character and volume. Always compare both radial pulses, and feel the radial and femoral together to look for delay. Peripheral pulses to know: **radial, brachial, carotid, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial**. Never palpate both carotid arteries at the same time.

### Measuring the JVP

1. Position the patient at **45 degrees** with the neck relaxed and the head turned slightly **away** from the side being examined.
2. Look for the **internal jugular vein** pulsation (a double waveform, not palpable, obliterated by pressing at the base of the neck, and changing with posture and breathing).
3. Measure the **vertical** height of the top of the pulsation above the **sternal angle** (the bony ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum).
4. A JVP up to about **3 cm above the sternal angle** is normal. Because the right atrium lies about **5 cm below the sternal angle**, a JVP of 3 cm above corresponds to about 8 cm above the right atrium.

blocks.caption: h is the vertical height of the venous column above the sternal angle in cm; 5 cm is the conventional distance from the sternal angle to the right atrium.

blocks.title: Converting a JVP height
blocks.prompt: A patient reclined at 45 degrees has the top of the venous pulsation 6 cm vertically above the sternal angle. Estimate the pressure above the right atrium and say whether it is normal.

steps.text: Add the conventional 5 cm from the sternal angle to the right atrium.
Compare with the normal upper limit of about 3 cm above the sternal angle (about 8 cm above the right atrium).
11 cm is above 8 cm and 6 cm is above 3 cm, so the JVP is raised.

blocks.answer: About 11 cm above the right atrium; the JVP is raised.

blocks.markdown:
### Precordium: inspection and palpation

Expose the chest. **Inspect** for scars (for example a midline sternotomy), visible pulsations and chest wall deformity. **Palpate** the **apex beat**, the lowest and most lateral point where the cardiac impulse can be felt. Normally it is in the **fifth intercostal space, in the midclavicular line**. Displacement to the left suggests an enlarged left ventricle. Then feel for **heaves** (a sustained lift of the sternum, as in right ventricular enlargement) and **thrills** (palpable murmurs).

blocks.caption: The four auscultation areas (surface markings of where each valve's sound is best heard)
rows: Second intercostal space, right sternal edge
Second intercostal space, left sternal edge
Fourth or fifth intercostal space, left sternal edge
Apex, fifth intercostal space midclavicular line

blocks.markdown:
### The first and second heart sounds

Heart sounds are produced by the closure of heart valves, not by their opening in normal hearts.

- **First heart sound (S1)** is the closure of the **mitral and tricuspid** valves at the start of ventricular systole. It is loudest at the **apex**.
- **Second heart sound (S2)** is the closure of the **aortic and pulmonary** valves at the end of systole. It is loudest at the **base** (second intercostal spaces).

To tell which sound is which, feel the **carotid pulse** while auscultating: S1 coincides with the upstroke of the carotid pulse and S2 comes just after. Use the **diaphragm** for high-pitched sounds and the **bell** for low-pitched sounds.

blocks.title: Which sound is which?
blocks.prompt: You listen at the apex of a 40-year-old woman and hear two sounds per cycle, the first of which falls together with the carotid upstroke. Identify the first sound and say which valves produce it.

steps.text: Palpate the carotid at the same time as listening. The carotid upstroke occurs in early systole.
The sound that coincides with the upstroke is the first heart sound, S1.
S1 is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole.
The second sound, S2, follows the carotid pulse and marks the end of systole.

blocks.answer: The sound coinciding with the carotid upstroke is S1, from mitral and tricuspid valve closure.

items: Introduce yourself, gain consent, position the patient at 45 degrees and expose the chest.
General inspection and hands (clubbing, splinter haemorrhages).
Pulse rate and rhythm, then blood pressure.
Inspect and palpate the precordium, including the apex beat.
Auscultate in the four areas, with carotid timing.
Look for ankle and sacral oedema, and listen at the lung bases.

blocks.title: Apex beat is a landmark
blocks.text: A normal apex beat is in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. If you cannot feel it, say so; it can be hidden by obesity, emphysema or dextrocardia. Always describe its position and character.

blocks.title: Presenting the JVP
blocks.text: Report the height in cm above the sternal angle and whether the waveform is visible. State that it is measured at 45 degrees.

points: The cardiovascular examination follows a fixed order from general inspection through pulse, blood pressure and JVP to the precordium and signs of heart failure.
JVP is measured at 45 degrees as the vertical height above the sternal angle; up to about 3 cm is normal.
The apex beat is normally in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line; the four auscultation areas are aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid and mitral.
S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves (apex, coincides with carotid upstroke); S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves (loudest at the base).

questions.stem: At what angle should the patient lie when the JVP is assessed?

options.text: 45 degrees
Flat at 0 degrees
Upright at 90 degrees
Head down at -30 degrees

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the standard position for measuring the JVP.
distractorRationale.b: Flat positioning fills the veins and makes the top of the column hard to see.
distractorRationale.c: Upright positioning often hides a normal JVP below the clavicle.
distractorRationale.d: Head-down positioning overfills the neck veins.

questions.explanation: At 45 degrees a normal JVP is visible just above the clavicle and a raised JVP is readily seen. Measurement is always the vertical height above the sternal angle.

questions.stem: Which feature helps to distinguish the internal jugular venous pulsation from the carotid pulse?

options.text: It is not palpable and its level changes with posture and breathing
It is a single forceful outward beat that you can palpate
It is unaffected by pressure at the base of the neck
It becomes more prominent when the patient sits fully upright

questions.correctOptionText: It is not palpable and its level changes with posture and breathing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: venous pulsation is impalpable, biphasic and varies with posture and respiration.
distractorRationale.b: A single palpable beat describes the carotid.
distractorRationale.c: Pressing at the base of the neck obliterates the jugular pulsation.
distractorRationale.d: Sitting upright lowers the venous column, so it becomes less prominent.

questions.explanation: The jugular venous waveform is biphasic, impalpable, obliterable by pressure and altered by posture. The carotid pulse is palpable, single and unaffected by these manoeuvres.

questions.stem: A man is examined at 45 degrees. The top of the jugular venous pulsation is 2 cm vertically above the sternal angle. Using the convention that the right atrium lies 5 cm below the sternal angle, what is the venous pressure above the right atrium in cm?
questions.explanation: Add the 5 cm between the right atrium and the sternal angle to the 2 cm measured above the sternal angle, giving 7 cm. This is within the normal range, which is up to about 8 cm above the right atrium.

questions.stem: Where is a normal apex beat found?

options.text: Fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
Second intercostal space at the right sternal edge
Third intercostal space in the anterior axillary line
Seventh intercostal space in the midaxillary line

questions.correctOptionText: Fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line

distractorRationale.b: This is the aortic auscultation area.
distractorRationale.c: This is too high and lateral.
distractorRationale.d: This is too low and lateral.

questions.explanation: The apex beat is the lowest and most lateral cardiac impulse, normally fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. A displaced beat suggests ventricular enlargement.

questions.stem: Which auscultation area is located in the second intercostal space at the left sternal edge?

options.text: Pulmonary
Aortic
Mitral
Tricuspid

distractorRationale.a: Correct: second intercostal space, left sternal edge.
distractorRationale.b: The aortic area is on the right sternal edge.
distractorRationale.c: The mitral area is at the apex.
distractorRationale.d: The tricuspid area is at the lower left sternal edge.

questions.explanation: The aortic and pulmonary areas are mirror images in the second intercostal spaces, with the aortic on the right and the pulmonary on the left of the sternum.

questions.stem: A student palpates the carotid artery while listening at the apex. Two heart sounds are heard in each cycle. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The first sound coincides with the carotid upstroke
The second sound coincides with the carotid upstroke
Both sounds occur before the upstroke
The first sound is caused by opening of the semilunar valves

questions.correctOptionText: The first sound coincides with the carotid upstroke

distractorRationale.a: Correct: S1 marks the start of systole, so it coincides with the pulse.
distractorRationale.b: S2 comes after the carotid upstroke.
distractorRationale.c: Both sounds cannot precede the pulse.
distractorRationale.d: S1 is closure of the atrioventricular valves.

questions.explanation: The carotid pulse follows the start of ventricular ejection, so S1 (mitral and tricuspid closure) falls together with it. S2 (aortic and pulmonary closure) follows.

questions.stem: True or false: the second heart sound is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: S2 is produced by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole. Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves produces S1.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a palpable apex beat in the sixth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line. What is the most appropriate description of this finding?

options.text: The apex beat is displaced laterally and downward, suggesting left ventricular enlargement
The apex beat is normal
The apex beat is displaced upward and medially, suggesting a small heart
The apex beat is absent

questions.correctOptionText: The apex beat is displaced laterally and downward, suggesting left ventricular enlargement

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the position is lateral and lower than the fifth intercostal space midclavicular line.
distractorRationale.b: The normal position is fifth intercostal space midclavicular line.

questions.explanation: Compared with the normal fifth intercostal space midclavicular position, the sixth space in the anterior axillary line is further out and lower. This suggests dilatation of the left ventricle, although other causes of displacement exist.

questions.stem: Describe how you would assess the jugular venous pressure of a 70-year-old woman, including positioning, what you measure, and how you tell the venous pulse from the carotid pulse.
markingGuide: Consent and exposure of the neck
Patient at 45 degrees with head turned slightly away
Measure vertical height above the sternal angle
Normal up to about 3 cm above the sternal angle
Venous pulse is impalpable, biphasic, obliterated by pressure at the base and varies with posture and respiration
Carotid is palpable, single and unaffected by pressure at the base of the neck
questions.explanation: A complete answer links positioning to measurement and gives distinguishing features. The JVP is reported as a height above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.

questions.stem: Describe the four auscultation areas of the heart and explain how you would identify the first and second heart sounds in a 45-year-old man.
markingGuide: Aortic: second intercostal space right sternal edge
Pulmonary: second intercostal space left sternal edge
Mitral: apex, fifth intercostal space midclavicular line
S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, loudest at the apex
S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves, loudest at the base
Palpate the carotid pulse: S1 coincides with the upstroke
questions.explanation: Knowing both the surface positions and the physiological origin of each sound shows understanding rather than recall. Timing against the carotid pulse is the practical way to identify S1.
